[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Memory Mapping (memmap) for Large Datasets in NumPy"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"When working with datasets that exceed your computer's available RAM, traditional loading methods like np.load() or np.genfromdtxt() will cause Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors. NumPy provides memmap (memory mapping) to handle extremely large arrays efficiently without reading the entire file into memory at once."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"What is Memory Mapping?"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Memory mapping creates a connection between an array and a file on disk. Instead of loading the data into RAM, the operating system loads small segments (pages) into memory on demand when you access them, and writes them back when modified."},{"order":5,"type":"subheading","text":"Creating a Memory-Mapped File"},{"order":6,"type":"paragraph","text":"You can create a new memory-mapped file using np.memmap(). You need to specify the filename, data type, file mode, and the shape of the array."},{"order":7,"type":"code","text":"import numpy as np

# Define the dimensions of a massive dataset (e.g., 10,000 by 10,000 floats)
shape = (10000, 10000)
filename = 'large_data.dat'

# Create a memmap array backed by a file on disk
fp = np.memmap(filename, dtype='float32', mode='w+', shape=shape)

# Write some data to a specific slice
fp[0:1000, :] = 1.5

# Flush changes to disk
fp.flush()"},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"Opening an Existing Memory-Mapped File"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"If the file already exists on disk, you can open it in read-only ('r') or read-write ('r+') mode. This allows you to analyze data instantly without waiting for disk-to-RAM loading times."},{"order":10,"type":"code","text":"# Open an existing memmap file in read-only mode
read_fp = np.memmap('large_data.dat', dtype='float32', mode='r', shape=(10000, 10000))

# Access a slice of data seamlessly
subset = read_fp[500:510, 500:510]
print(subset)"},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"File Modes Overview"},{"order":12,"type":"bullet_point","text":"'r': Read-only. The file must already exist."},{"order":13,"type":"bullet_point","text":"'w+': Create or truncate existing file. Destroys existing data and opens for reading and writing."},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"'r+': Open an existing file for reading and writing."},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"'c': Copy-on-write. Changes are made to memory locally and are not saved to disk."},{"order":16,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practices and Gotchas"},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Always call .flush() when modifying data to ensure changes are written back to disk."},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Non-contiguous slicing operations can cause performance bottlenecks because the OS must fetch scattered memory pages."},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Always ensure the dtype and shape match the underlying file specification exactly, or you will experience data corruption or dimension errors."}]
